question: Am I obliged to attend Jumu'ah and the masjid once it reopens after the coronavirus lockdown?
asked: In light of the announcement that a number of masajid across the country will be opening: what if an individual does not feel comfortable, because of their individual circumstances or because of the inadequacy of the situation and the conditions? Are they still obliged to go pray in the masjid?
answer:
So realize, dear brothers and sisters, that praying the five prayers in the masajid, the default position within the four schools of Islamic law is that it is strongly encouraged, and that communities should make sure that there's something going on, but it is not obligatory on individuals. Now, there is a position that says that it is obligatory on individuals if they live close to the masjid, and that position is a good one; it's there. But the default and the majority is that the daily salah can be prayed anywhere. And so it is not an individual obligation, fard 'ayn, for the person to go to the masjid, and that is the vast majority of scholars from our Islamic history.

The real issue is not the individual salah; the real issue is Jumu'ah salah, the Friday prayer. Because, as we are all aware, the Friday prayer, the default position is that it is obligatory upon adult Muslim males if they are able to come and pray. Now that the communities are opening, or some communities are opening, the question arises: should individuals who are worried about their individual circumstances come and pray?

And the response is that really this is a two-part question, or a two-party question, not two-part. And that is that every single person needs to look first and foremost at himself or herself, and then at the community that they are a part of and the precautions that are being taken, and the area and the locality that they're living in. This is not a specific answer that I can give to all of the Muslims across America, much less across the globe. Rather, it is case by case. Individuals need to assess both their own situation and the situation of the land and the ambience of the masjid that they are wishing to pray in, and take into account all of these factors, and then, based upon that, take a judicious position.

Let me state that the default is that if, number one, their health is overall... they're healthy, there's no symptoms, and they're of the age group, because again, the age does play a role here. All governmental agencies, the World Health Organization, are saying that those that are above the age of 65, or even 60, some are saying, represent a much higher risk. And so obviously, if you're in that age group above 65, or you have other underlying conditions and you need to take precautions, in this case, inshaAllah ta'ala, no matter what the situation is outside of the house, if you yourself are socially distancing and isolating yourself for medical reasons as it is, then inshaAllah ta'ala you are not obliged to go for Jumu'ah. If you have an underlying condition, or you are very senior in your age, and therefore the problems are compounded for your particular demographic, then definitely Jumu'ah is not obligatory.

However, if you are of regular, sound health, and in the community that you're living in and the land that you're living in the alert level has gone down slightly, which is what is happening across the globe after our social distancing, and your masjid is taking reasonable precautions, then indeed the default would be that Jumu'ah does become obligatory, as it was before the coronavirus lockdown took place. And so if you do fit all of these conditions, then the general ruling is that you should go.

Now, if any of these conditions is not met (you individually are not of a healthy demographic, or your land, your city, is still in the high-risk zone, or your masjid is not taking reasonable precautions, and there's only one masjid in the city and that masjid is really not understanding what is going on), when you are aware that the situation is not reasonable at this time to do what the masjid is doing, you do have in this case a legitimate excuse.

But remember, you have to answer to Allah on the Day of Judgment. I cannot specifically tell you; you have to think about your own situation and make an educated guess. All I'm doing is giving you the overall tools: if you feel that there is a legitimate fear. Because again, the Shari'ah does take into account legitimate fear. It does not take into account that which is atypical, that which is not going to be realistic. What is called the preponderance of the circumstance, ghalabat al-zann: if you think that there is a reasonable doubt that you might possibly fall sick, or the environment is not conducive for that, then inshaAllah ta'ala you have the Islamic permissibility to not attend Jumu'ah, and you will then pray Dhuhr in your house.

However, generally speaking, we here in the state of Texas, as you know, in Dallas in particular, our own masjid, East Plano, will be opening up inshaAllah this week. And we will be taking reasonable precautions: social distancing, shortening the Jumu'ah prayer timings. There's no intermingling of the musalleen. Everybody will be praying six feet apart, and so many other protocols that we're taking into account. People will bring their own individual prayer rugs. They're going to be wearing masks. So with all of these precautions in place, and if you are of a healthy demographic in this vicinity, **my position would be that it is obligatory for you to now come back for Jumu'ah, now that the situation has indeed changed.**
